newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Defiant Spanish communist brands critics as "nuns".
newsitem.headline: Defiant Spanish communist brands critics as "nuns".

text.p: Spain's communist party chief, who kicked up a storm in Madrid by questioning the future of the hugely popular monarchy, accused his detractors on Wednesday of acting like startled nuns who had sensed a sin.
"There are people in my country who believe that Spain is like a convent...and that there are things you cannot say," Julio Anguita said.

"You cannot talk of a republic and other things because God will punish you," the defiant leftist leader told a news conference after a two-day trip to Lisbon during which he held talks with local Communist leaders and met the President of republican Portugal.

Describing the reaction to his remarks as "hysterical", Anguita, who also leads the United Left (IU) coalition in parliament, said that the Communists had always been republicans despite backing the restoration of the monarchy after the death of rightwing dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

In a speech in Spain last weekend, Anguita said that the Communists felt no obligation to continue supporting the 1978 constitution, enshrining the role of the monarchy, if rival political parties went on ignoring other duties laid down in the charter.

He stepped up the heat further on Monday by accusing King Juan Carlos, revered by Spaniards for his part in consolidating democracy, with exceeding his role when he made approving comments recently about European monetary union and Nato -- two things the Communists fiercely oppose.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar dismissed any suggestion of Spain reverting to a republic as absurd, adding that he was not even prepared to debate the issue.
"The immense majority of Spaniards, and I'm among them, won't participate with the criteria that he (Anguita) has placed on the table," Aznar said.

Anguita said that the ruling conservative Popular Party and the Socialists that it replaced in elections last March had ridden roughshod over constitutional commitments to boost employment and guarantee the equal rights of all Spaniards.

The Communists, the biggest voice in the IU, Spain's third largest political grouping, are furious at the government's defiance of court requests to hand over secret files on a 1980s "dirty war" which the Socialists are alleged to have waged against violent Basque separatists.

Portuguese Communist Party leader Carlos Carvalhas told journalists that the two leftist parties would cooperate on a range of issues, including pressing for a referendum in both countries on whether to join an European single currency.
